A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EB-JDAT research, and their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. All pages were inspected, including v1's Appendices A and B; v2 ends with references and contains no appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification, adversarial robustness, generation, energy-distribution, and gradient-weight ablation results.

after.justification: v2 reports original CIFAR results, ImageNet-subset experiments, revised gradient-weight ablations, and a new adversarial-sampling-step study.

M1.justification: The joint-energy framework remains, but its default training procedure changes substantially. Section 3.3 replaces perceptual-loss-based naturalness constraints with perturbation-set-constrained adversarial sampling and removes the LPIPS term. Default gradient weights change from (0.45, 0.05, 0.45) to (1, 1, 1). A perceptual-loss-free variant already appeared in v1, so this is a revision of the default procedure rather than an entirely new framework.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. v2 additionally uses the first 100 ImageNet classes, reporting classification and robustness results in Table 4 and generated 64-by-64 images in Figure 3. This extends empirical coverage beyond CIFAR, although it does not constitute full ImageNet evaluation.

E2.justification: Within Table 2, v2 removes PGD-AT, TRADES, and VART and adds UIAT, SGLR, and DHAT-CFA. PGD-AT and TRADES remain in other analyses, so they are not removed throughout the paper. The broader JEM, energy-based AT, and generated-data comparator families remain.

E3.justification: The stated architecture for conventional AT comparisons changes from WRN34-10 to WRN28-10, matching EB-JDAT's stated backbone. Default gradient weights also change. New protocols cover the first 100 ImageNet classes with training images resized to 64-by-64 and sampling-step variation with fixed perturbation budget and step size. Table 3 drops the 50M-generated-image, 1600-epoch Better DM setting. These are reported protocol changes, not proof that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v1's five-setting gradient-weight ablation is replaced by four different configurations in v2 Table 6, changing the component controls and removing the classification-gradient-free case. v2 adds Figure 5, testing 1, 5, 10, and 20 adversarial sampling steps against performance, collapse, and runtime. The explicit perceptual-loss versus no-perceptual-loss comparison in v1 Table 3 disappears.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty across runs. Table 1 retains the same energy-difference mean and variance reporting; this describes sample distributions rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added. Table 2's SADAJEM-based CIFAR-10 clean/PGD/AA results change from 92.28/66.12/64.76 to 90.39/68.76/66.30 under revised defaults; 66.30 AA already appeared for v1's perceptual-loss-free variant. The SADAJEM baseline FID changes from 11.40 to 17.38. v2 adds ImageNet results, including 32.40 AA, and new ablation and timing results. Its introduction incorrectly identifies 68.76 as AutoAttack accuracy, contradicting Table 2.

T1.justification: The joint-probability factorization and principal gradient approximations remain. Equations 11–12 revise the mathematical adversarial-sampling formulation from a naturalness/perceptual constraint to a perturbation-set constraint, and v1's explicit LPIPS distance definition is removed. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that joint energy modeling aligns clean, adversarial, and generated distributions, supports multiple JEM variants, and combines strong robustness with near-original classification and generation quality. The expanded experiments and updated headline numbers support the same central contribution rather than redefining it.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explicit interpretation of the remaining trade-off: adversarial regularization can shift probability mass away from the clean manifold and reduce sample fidelity. It revises the gradient-component interpretation and explains sampling steps through attack strength versus collapse risk. The high-dimensional training limitation remains, while v1's misuse and safeguards discussion is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds GPU-hour estimates, per-epoch timing, explicit attack norms and AutoAttack components, and ImageNet preprocessing information. It retains the RTX 3090 disclosure in the main text but removes Appendix B's CPU, memory, PyTorch, and explicit validation-configuration information. The explicit ten-step generative-sampling setting is replaced by a reference to JEM defaults.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for UIAT, SGLR, DHAT-CFA, ImageNet, FAB, Square Attack, and feature-denoising work, while removing the LPIPS and VART references. The related-work narrative and positioning relative to JEMs and adversarial training remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and parts of the introduction are rewritten, motivation and ablation discussions gain subheadings, Section 5 is retitled, and the appendices are removed with some details retained elsewhere. Richang Hong is added to the author list. The main six-section narrative and much of the prose remain.

P2.justification: v2 reformats the paper into two columns, redraws and relocates the robustness scatterplot to the first page, adds ImageNet samples and a sampling-step radar chart, and adds an ImageNet table. Existing tables gain runtime or AA columns, while the ablation table is restructured. The energy histograms and CIFAR sample grids are retained through renumbering and relocation.

improvement.justification: The ImageNet-subset evaluation, matched stated comparison backbones, and new sampling-step study provide useful additional support for generality and training stability beyond v1's CIFAR experiments. The explicit discussion of residual generation trade-offs also improves interpretation. These gains are limited by removed implementation details and stronger-budget Better DM comparisons, plus the new headline error labeling 68.76% as AutoAttack accuracy when Table 2 reports 66.30%.
